newsitem.title: USA: Fewer hospital stays for asthma users of steroid.
newsitem.headline: Fewer hospital stays for asthma users of steroid.

text.p: Asthma sufferers who treated their lung inflammation with steroid inhalants reduced the chance they would need to go to a hospital to deal with a breathing attack, researchers said on Tuesday.

In a study of nearly 17,000 asthma patients, researchers at Brigham and Women's Hospital in Boston found a 50 percent decrease in the risk of emergency room or hospital stays among steroid users compared to patients prescribed only a commonly used inhalant or no treatment at all.

The study found that moderate users of the common inhalants known as beta-agonists, which ease the symptoms of an asthma attack, also had a reduced risk of hospital visits compared to untreated asthmatics.
But heavy users, with at least eight prescriptions of beta-agonists a year, had four times the risk of needing hospital treatment, a risk that declined markedly if they also used steroid inhalants.

"Our results support recommendations that individuals with moderate to severe asthma should include inhaled steroids as part of their regular therapeutic regime," James Donahue wrote in the Journal of the American Medical Association.

A recent study that appeared in the March 4 issue of the Journal warned that heavy doses of steroid inhalants could be linked to glaucoma, although the study's authors continued to recommend their use in moderation.

About 40 percent of the asthma patients in the latest study were receiving the inhaled steroids, and 86 percent were prescribed beta-agonists. Cromolyn, a non-steroidal inhalant often preferred for children, was also found to provide protection for its younger users, the researchers said.
The study was partly funded by British pharmaceutical company Zeneca Group Plc. The report did not identify the makers of the steroid inhalants.
